findings.description: charge() (StripePaymentGateway.java:139-144) maps every StripeException to a single PaymentGatewayException("payment.lifecycleFailure"), with no outcome-unknown classification — unlike refund() in the same class, which treats ApiConnectionException / status 0 / 409 / 5xx as 'may have executed'. If PaymentIntent.create times out or returns 5xx after Stripe actually captured the charge, handleCreditBasedBooking's catch (PaymentLifecycleService.java:254-259) calls persistPaymentFailure, whose loadOrCreate picks up the committed CAPTURE_PENDING reservation row and overwrites it to CHARGE_FAILED with creditDebited=0/stripeCharged=0, transitions the booking to DECLINED and notifies the parent nothing was charged. The batch path (PaymentLifecycleService.java:389-403) does the same for every reserved booking and additionally reverses the credit deduction. The parent's card is charged while the only durable record says no money moved — and because the row is now terminal CHARGE_FAILED rather than CAPTURE_PENDING, PaymentPendingSweeper's CAPTURE_UNCONFIRMED escalation can never fire, so nothing is ever reconciled; the never-re-charge guard in abortSettle protects exactly this window on a crash, but the timeout path bypasses it.
findings.title: Unknown-outcome Stripe charge is recorded as CHARGE_FAILED, overwriting the CAPTURE_PENDING reservation
findings.verification: Confirm no reconciliation job scans Stripe PaymentIntents (by transfer_group / referenceId metadata) against CHARGE_FAILED booking_payments rows; grep for consumers of 'payment.lifecycleFailure' that distinguish outcome-unknown. Also confirm the Stripe SDK's built-in retry (same idempotency key) does not fully eliminate the exhausted-retries/5xx case — it does not.

findings.description: The BOOKING_DEDUCTION ledger entry (line 380, via writeLedgerEntry, @Transactional REQUIRED) joins the listener's REQUIRES_NEW transaction, which only commits after the whole settle loop; each confirmCreditBatchPayment (line 434) commits immediately in perBookingTx (REQUIRES_NEW, a second connection). If the JVM dies — e.g. a deploy's SIGTERM after the 8s graceful-drain window — between the first confirm's commit and the outer commit, the CAPTURED booking_payments rows recording creditDebited>0 and the CONFIRMED bookings survive while the wallet debit rolls back: the parent keeps both the credit and the sessions, and nothing detects it (no CAPTURE_PENDING rows remain for the confirmed bookings, so the sweeper sees nothing). The same crash after a failed confirm's declineBatchBookingAfterCharge (REQUIRES_NEW, committed) refunds the parent a credit share that was never debited. Contrast the single-booking path, where persistPaymentSuccess writes ledger + payment row + transition in one transaction precisely to avoid this.
findings.title: Batch credit deduction commits in the outer transaction while per-booking CAPTURED confirms commit in REQUIRES_NEW — a restart loses the debit but keeps the sessions
findings.verification: Confirm CreditWalletService.writeLedgerEntry is plain @Transactional (REQUIRED — verified in CreditWalletService.java:191-194) and that no outbox or reconciliation compares the sum of CAPTURED creditDebited per batch against BOOKING_DEDUCTION ledger rows for the batchId.

findings.description: The sweep loads all PaymentCoachSubscription rows in one transaction (line 1009) and then, in each per-row transaction, computes the entitled tier from that detached snapshot's tier/status without re-reading the payment row under any lock (lines 1015-1037); syncMarketplaceTier locks only coach_profiles. If persistCoachTierUpgrade commits tier=ACADEMY (and syncs the projection) between the batch load and that coach's iteration, the sweep compares the projection (ACADEMY) against the stale expectation (INSTRUCTOR), declares a mismatch, and overwrites the projection back to INSTRUCTOR — a lost update that downgrades the coach's marketplace entitlement until the next sweep run or the next entitlement-changing event. The same shape applies to a concurrent revoke (projection forced back up to a paid tier the coach just lost).
findings.title: reconcileMarketplaceTiers writes the marketplace projection from a stale pre-sweep snapshot, reverting a concurrently committed tier change
findings.verification: Confirm the scheduler cadence for reconcileMarketplaceTiers (the longer the interval, the longer the wrong tier persists) and that CoachSubscription has no @Version that would reject the stale write — CoachSubscriptionRepository.findByCoachId takes no lock.

findings.description: The guard reads stripe_customers.stripePaymentMethodId (lines 608-614) and only then issues the Stripe updates, with nothing serialising two syncs for the same user. If a user saves card A then card B in quick succession: instance 1 claims sync-A and passes the check before card B's save commits, then stalls; instance 2 claims sync-B, completes, and sets B as every subscription's default_payment_method; instance 1 resumes and sets A. The database says B is the saved card while Stripe renews against the replaced card A indefinitely — no later event re-runs the sync, so it never converges; if A is subsequently detached or expires, renewals fail into dunning/PAST_DUE for a user who did update their card. The per-key idempotency (sub-pm-{subId}-{pmId}) only dedupes replays of the same card, not the A/B interleaving.
findings.title: Payment-method sync outbox: superseded-card check is not atomic with the Stripe writes, so two syncs on two instances can leave Stripe billing the replaced card
findings.verification: Check PaymentMethodSyncOutboxHandler / the outbox claim mechanism: if it processes rows for the same aggregate strictly serially and in enqueue order across instances (e.g. per-user partitioning or a user-level lock), the interleaving is closed and this is not a finding.

findings.description: Both helpers (lines 1480-1496) do an unlocked findByCoachId/findByPlayerId and insert on miss, with no upsert and no catch. Two concurrent first requests for the same coach (e.g. GET /subscription racing POST /subscribe, or a double-fired page load) both miss the read before either insert commits; the loser's transaction dies on the coach_id/player_id unique constraint and the request surfaces a 500 from what is otherwise a read endpoint (getCoachSubscription is @Transactional around the create). Harm is bounded to one failed request — the constraint itself prevents a duplicate row — but the path has no retry or on-conflict handling.
findings.title: findOrCreateCoachSubscription / findOrCreatePlayerSubscription race two first-touch requests into a unique-constraint failure
findings.verification: Confirm the unique index on payment.coach_subscriptions(coach_id) and payment.player_subscriptions(player_id) exists in the Flyway migrations (the entity declares unique=true but DDL is migration-managed), and that no controller-level advice retries DataIntegrityViolationException here.
